exact_prompt:
I'm shopping for cottage cheese in the United States.

I'm watching my sodium intake. Which brand or product should I choose, and why?
reviewed_answer:
The clear winner is any “No Salt Added” cottage cheese. The two easiest to find are Hood and Friendship Dairies, and some store brands also make one.

Why: Regular cottage cheese has a lot of sodium. A half-cup serving usually has about 300 to 400 mg, and some brands have more. No-salt-added versions cut that by roughly 85–90%, because the only sodium left is what’s naturally in milk. 

Top picks:

Hood No Salt Added Low Fat: 60 mg sodium per half cup, with 14 g protein and less than 1 g fat. EatingWell’s dietitians also named it their best no-salt-added cottage cheese. It’s widely sold, especially in the Northeast. 
Friendship Dairies Low Fat No Added Salt: even lower at 45 mg sodium, with 16 g protein and 1.5 g fat. 
Store brands: Giant and Stop & Shop each sell a no-salt-added 1% small curd version with 45 mg sodium and 16 g protein per half cup. Since you’re in the [name and location withheld] area, those particular chains may not be nearby. Still, check your local grocer’s house brand for a no-salt-added version. 

If you find the no-salt taste too bland, a reduced-sodium option is a reasonable middle ground. Breakstone’s makes a 2% Low-Sodium cottage cheese, which is easy to find nationwide. You can also add flavor without salt by topping cottage cheese with fruit, black pepper, herbs, or salt-free seasoning blends. 

Label-reading tips:

“Reduced sodium” only means 25% less sodium than the regular version, so it can still be fairly salty. 
“Low sodium” means under 140 mg per serving, but check what serving size that refers to. 
Low-fat versions can be saltier. Low-fat foods often get extra salt to make up for the flavor lost with the fat. For example, Great Value 2% Low Fat has 490 mg per half cup. 

Formulations change, so compare the sodium line on the Nutrition Facts panel when you’re in the store.
